In 'His memory is a sieve,' explicitly name the figure of speech and explain the comparison.
The figure of speech is a metaphor.
It suggests he forgets things as a sieve lets material pass through.
This is metaphor: things slip from his memory as they slip through holes in a sieve.
It is a literal scientific claim that his brain is a metal kitchen tool.
In 'The lake was like glass,' explicitly name the figure of speech and explain the shared quality.
The figure of speech is a simile.
The comparison suggests the lake's surface is smooth or still like glass.
It is a simile comparing the calm, smooth water with glass.
The sentence literally says the entire lake has turned into solid glass, with no comparison.
In 'The wind whispered through the trees,' explicitly name the figure of speech and identify the human action.
The figure of speech is personification.
Whispering is the human action attributed to the wind.
This is personification because the wind is given the human act of speaking in a whisper.
It is a literal report of a human inside every tree, and no action is attributed to wind.
In 'I waited a thousand years for the bus,' explicitly name the exaggeration device and explain the intended meaning.
The device is hyperbole.
The speaker means the wait felt very long, not that a thousand years literally passed.
The hyperbole conveys an unbearably long-feeling wait rather than an actual millennium.
This is an exact historical measurement proving the speaker is more than one thousand years old.
An organizer tells a joke to 'break the ice' at a first meeting. Explain the idiom and identify the situation in which it is used here.
The idiom means to reduce awkwardness or make people feel at ease.
Here it is used when people first meet.
The joke helps people relax, in the setting of an initial meeting.
The organizer must smash frozen water during a meeting that never takes place.
'Alex told Sam that he had won.' State the two possible referents of 'he'.
He could refer to Alex.
He could refer to Sam.
Either Alex or Sam may be the person who won.
He can only refer to a third person called Lee who is never mentioned.
'The roads were icy, so the match was postponed.' Identify the stated cause and result.
The icy roads are the stated cause.
Postponing the match is the result.
Ice on the roads leads to the decision to put off the match.
Postponement causes the earlier ice, and the match takes place as originally scheduled.
Compare 'Mina was tired, but she continued' with 'Mina was tired, and she was hungry.' State the relation marked by each connective.
But marks a contrast between tiredness and continuing.
And adds the information that Mina was hungry.
The first links contrasting ideas; the second adds another condition alongside tiredness.
But means simple addition and and signals that hunger contradicts tiredness.
'A vase stood beside a book. The vase fell and shattered. This upset Jo.' What does 'this' refer to, and who is upset?
This refers to the vase falling and shattering.
Jo is upset.
The breakage of the vase is what this points back to, and Jo is the person distressed.
This means the book was repaired, and the text says only Mina was upset.
Explain the difference between 'Let's eat, Grandma' and 'Let's eat Grandma'.
With the comma, Grandma is being addressed as someone invited to eat.
Without the comma, the wording presents Grandma as what will be eaten.
The comma makes Grandma the addressee; omitting it makes her the grammatical object of eating.
Both sentences unambiguously mean that Grandma has already eaten and nobody is speaking to her.
'Lena said, “The bridge is safe.” The narrator added that no inspection had occurred.' Identify Lena's claim and the narrator's statement.
Lena claims the bridge is safe.
The narrator states that it has not been inspected.
Safety is Lena's assertion; the absence of an inspection is information supplied by the narrator.
The narrator guarantees safety after an inspection, while Lena says the bridge is closed.
'The garden needs water: its soil is dry and its leaves are wilting.' Identify the claim and the supporting observations.
The claim is that the garden needs water.
Dry soil and wilting leaves are the supporting observations.
The writer argues for watering, citing the dry earth and drooping leaves as evidence.
The claim is that the garden is flooded, supported by soaked soil and upright leaves.
A writer sees one dog swim and claims every dog loves water. State what the observation supports and why the broader claim is too strong.
It shows that the observed dog swam.
One example does not establish a preference shared by every dog.
The evidence concerns one swimming dog; it cannot prove all dogs enjoy water.
The observation proves that no dog can swim and that all dogs dislike water.
'Ari put on a coat and picked up an umbrella.' Give one explicit action and one plausible but unproven inference about the weather.
Ari explicitly picked up an umbrella.
Rain may be expected, but the passage does not establish that it is raining.
The text directly says Ari took an umbrella; expecting rain is a reasonable possibility rather than a proven weather report.
The passage explicitly states that snow is falling and that Ari left the umbrella behind.
'All three lamps in the room are off.' State what is established about those lamps and whether this proves the entire building is dark.
The three lamps in the specified room are off.
The sentence does not establish that the whole building is dark.
Only those room lamps are said to be off; lighting elsewhere in the building remains unspecified.
Every lamp in the building is definitely on and the sentence proves that every room is dark.
Summarize: 'The new route is faster during quiet hours, but heavy traffic can remove that advantage.' Retain the benefit and its qualification.
The route can be faster in quiet traffic.
Heavy traffic can eliminate the speed advantage.
It saves time when traffic is light, but that saving can disappear when traffic becomes heavy.
The route is always faster in all traffic and can never lose its advantage.
The passage says a library opens at nine. A summary adds 'which is much too late.' Identify the source fact and the added opinion.
Opening at nine is the fact supplied by the passage.
Calling that time much too late is an added judgment.
Nine o'clock comes from the source, while disapproving of that opening time is the summarizer's own evaluation.
The passage says the library never opens and supplies the exact opinion that nine is too early.
Compare 'The door is locked' with 'The door is not locked'. Explain each sentence's claim.
The first asserts that the door is locked.
The second denies that it is locked.
One says the lock is engaged; the other says that is not the case.
Both statements say the door has been physically removed and make no claim about locking.
Contrast 'The parcel may arrive today' and 'The parcel will arrive today' in the certainty expressed.
May presents arrival today as a possibility.
Will presents arrival today as an asserted expectation or prediction.
The first allows arrival as possible, whereas the second states it as what is expected to happen.
May guarantees delivery already happened yesterday, while will denies every possibility of delivery.
Distinguish 'Some players are tired' from 'All players are tired'. State the scope of each.
Some says at least part of the group is tired without asserting that every player is.
All says every player in the group is tired.
The first asserts tiredness for at least some members, while the second extends it to the entire group.
Some means nobody is tired and all means exactly one player is tired.
'You may enter only if you have a pass.' State the necessary condition and whether the sentence guarantees entry to every pass holder.
Having a pass is necessary for entry.
The sentence does not by itself guarantee entry to everyone with a pass.
Entry requires a pass, but possessing one is not stated to be a complete guarantee of admission.
No pass is needed and every person without one is guaranteed entry.
'Return every borrowed item except the red folder.' State what must be returned and which item is exempt.
All the other borrowed items must be returned.
The red folder is exempt from this return instruction.
Bring back the borrowed items other than the red folder, which the instruction excludes.
Keep all borrowed items and return only an unborrowed blue folder.
'Wash the cup before filling it.' State the first action and the later action.
Washing the cup comes first.
Filling the cup comes afterward.
The cup is washed, then it is filled.
Fill the cup first and the instruction forbids washing it afterward or beforehand.
'She sat on the bank and watched the river.' Explain 'bank' here and identify the contextual clue.
Bank means the land beside the river.
The reference to watching the river supports that meaning.
It is a riverbank, with the nearby mention of the river disambiguating the word.
Bank must mean a financial institution because the sentence contains no reference to water.
Compare 'work' in everyday 'I worked hard' with physics 'No work was done because there was no displacement.' Explain the two meanings.
Everyday work can mean effort or activity.
Mechanical work in physics requires an appropriate force component acting through displacement.
Ordinary speech can call effort work, while the physics quantity depends on force acting along movement.
Everyday work always means exactly force times displacement, while physics work means any feeling of tiredness.
In a short poem, 'Come home' begins every stanza. Identify the repeated phrase and one plausible effect.
The repeated phrase is Come home.
Repetition can emphasize longing or urgency for someone's return.
Repeating Come home at each stanza opening stresses the speaker's wish for a return.
The phrase is never repeated and the poem explicitly celebrates wanting nobody to return.
In 'silver snakes slide silently,' explicitly name the repeated initial-sound device and identify the repeated sound.
The device is alliteration.
The initial /s/ sound is repeated.
This is alliteration built around repeated s sounds at the starts of words.
It is a rhyme based on every word ending with the sound of cat.
'The sharp scent of pine filled the cold air.' Identify the main sense evoked by 'scent' and quote the source of that scent.
It appeals to the sense of smell.
Pine is the stated source of the scent.
The line evokes smelling, specifically the odor of pine.
The line appeals only to sight and says the smell comes from oranges.
'The empty hall echoed. “How peaceful,” I thought.' Distinguish one atmosphere suggested by the hall from the speaker's stated attitude.
The empty echoing hall can suggest a lonely or quiet atmosphere.
The speaker regards it as peaceful.
The setting can feel solitary and quiet, while the narrator explicitly welcomes its peace.
The hall is described as crowded and noisy, and the speaker explicitly calls it terrifying.
'We cheered as the gates opened. Then we saw the wreckage and fell silent.' Identify the tone before and after the discovery.
The opening tone is excited or celebratory.
The later tone is shocked or somber.
Joy at the opening gives way to subdued shock on seeing the damage.
The speakers are silent with grief at first and celebrate the wreckage afterward.
'No one was watching, yet Noor returned the lost wallet.' Infer one trait and identify the action supporting it.
The action suggests honesty.
Noor returns a lost wallet even without an audience.
Noor seems honest, as shown by giving the wallet back when nobody is watching.
Noor clearly steals the wallet for applause, demonstrating that nobody ever returns it.
Distinguish the narrator of a fictional story from its author.
The narrator is the voice or figure that tells the story.
The author is the person who creates the work.
The story's telling voice is its narrator; the real writer who constructs the work is its author.
Every fictional narrator is automatically the real author, and no distinction can exist.

A first-person narrator says, 'I waited outside the closed meeting-room door and could neither see nor hear what happened inside.' State what the narrator directly experiences and one limit on their knowledge.
The narrator directly experiences waiting outside.
The account does not give direct access to what is happening inside the meeting.
The speaker knows their own wait, but events beyond the closed door are outside their direct observation.
The narrator directly sees every action inside the room and never waits outside.
A narrator says, 'I never read the letter,' but later admits reading that same letter. Identify the contradiction and its effect on reliability.
The denial of reading conflicts with the later admission of reading it.
The contradiction gives reason to question the narrator's reliability.
The narrator first denies reading the letter then admits doing so, which undermines confidence in the account.
The statements fully agree and prove the narrator can never be unreliable.
The audience sees a hidden trap, while a character walks toward it unaware. State the audience's knowledge and the character's knowledge.
The audience knows the trap is there.
The character does not know about the trap.
Viewers see the danger, but the approaching character remains unaware of it.
The character knows about the trap while the audience has been told nothing about it.
A story first shows a frayed rope; later it breaks during a climb. Identify the earlier clue and explain the connection to the later event.
The earlier clue is the rope's frayed condition.
That damage anticipates the rope breaking during the climb.
The initial wear on the rope hints at the failure that happens later.
The earlier clue is a brand-new steel bridge, and the rope never breaks.
For a tale in which a boastful runner loses after resting too long, distinguish a plot detail from a possible theme.
Losing after an overlong rest is a plot event.
Overconfidence can lead to failure is a possible theme.
The runner's loss following a long rest belongs to the events; the warning about overconfidence is a broader idea.
The plot is that nobody ever runs, and the only possible theme is that overconfidence always guarantees success.
A character carries a key after leaving a childhood home and calls it 'a piece of where I belong.' Identify the object and a supported symbolic meaning.
The object is a key.
It can symbolize connection to home or belonging.
The key is the object, representing the character's continuing tie to home.
The object is a map explicitly symbolizing hatred of every home and relationship.
A story set during a present journey pauses to describe the narrator's childhood. Identify the shift and the earlier time being recalled.
The narrative shifts into a flashback.
The recalled events come from the narrator's childhood.
A flashback interrupts the journey to revisit the speaker's early years.
The story jumps to a guaranteed future event and never mentions the past.
'You forgot again.' 'I know. I'm sorry.' Give a supported relationship tension and the second speaker's response.
The first speaker expresses frustration at a repeated lapse.
The second speaker acknowledges it and apologizes.
One speaker is annoyed that it has happened again; the other accepts the complaint and says sorry.
Both speakers deny any mistake and respond by congratulating each other.
Compare 'Please inform me of your decision' with 'Let me know what you pick.' Identify which wording is more formal and whether the two sentences request different actions.
Please inform me of your decision is more formal.
Both ask the other person to communicate their decision.
The inform-me wording is more formal; both versions ask the listener to tell the speaker what they decide.
Both are identical in wording and neither expresses a request for a decision.
You describe a scientific result to specialists and to young children. Give an appropriate vocabulary choice for each audience.
A specialist audience may understand precise technical terminology.
Young children may need familiar words and explanations of unfamiliar terms.
Experts can use the field's technical vocabulary; children benefit from everyday language with new terms explained.
Children always require unexplained advanced jargon, while specialists can never understand any technical term.
Correct 'She go to school every day' in standard present-tense English and identify the grammatical person and number of its subject.
The corrected sentence is She goes to school every day.
The subject she is third-person singular.
The sentence should read She goes to school every day, and she denotes a third-person singular subject.
The correction is She go to school every day; she is first-person plural.
Choose 'is' or 'are' in 'The list of names ___ on the desk' and identify the head of the subject controlling agreement.
The correct choice is is.
List is the singular head of the subject.
Use is because list, rather than names, is the subject's singular head.
Use are because desk is the plural subject.
Compare 'Close the window' and 'Could you please close the window?' State their shared requested action and the politeness difference.
Both request closing the window.
The second is phrased more politely or indirectly.
They ask for the same window-closing action, with the question form adding a more polite, indirect request.
The first asks to open the window, while the second forbids closing it and is necessarily an insult.
Why can translating 'spill the beans' word for word mislead a reader? Give the idiomatic meaning and the literal image.
The idiom means to reveal a secret.
The literal words describe scattering beans out of a container.
Its intended meaning is disclosing secret information, although the words literally picture beans being spilled.
The idiom means to keep every secret forever and literally describes painting a wall.
Paraphrase 'Mira did not send the letter yesterday' while preserving the negation and time reference.
The paraphrase must retain that Mira did not send the letter.
It must retain yesterday as the stated time reference.
Yesterday, Mira did not send the letter.
Mira certainly mailed the letter tomorrow.
The original says 'Three students arrived after noon'; a paraphrase says 'People came.' Identify two specific details lost.
The exact count of three students is lost.
Arrival after noon is lost.
It drops the number and student identity, and it also drops the after-noon timing.
It loses the exact count of ten teachers and the statement that nobody arrived.
After repeated promises are broken, a speaker asks, 'How could I trust you now?' Explain its likely rhetorical purpose and whether it mainly asks for a factual procedure.
It expresses doubt or criticism about the person's trustworthiness.
It is mainly rhetorical rather than a request for step-by-step factual instructions.
The question voices distrust, serving as criticism instead of genuinely asking for a procedure.
It is an enthusiastic promise of complete trust and a literal request for a numbered repair manual.
'At last the room was silent. She smiled, then looked at the empty chair.' Give two defensible readings and the textual clue for each.
The smile can suggest relief or pleasure at the silence.
Looking at the empty chair can suggest awareness of someone's absence or loss.
Her smile supports relief, while her attention to the vacant chair supports a sense of absence.
The passage proves she is screaming at a crowded chair and gives no sign of silence or a smile.
